questions.article: As You Sow, So Shall You Reap
questions.q: The article says no one finds complete fulfilment in this world. What does it take this general discontent to be?
options: A fault in human nature
Not quite. The article says: A reminder that our true destination lies beyond this life.
A sign that people have too little
Not quite. The article says: A reminder that our true destination lies beyond this life.
A result of modern living
Not quite. The article says: A reminder that our true destination lies beyond this life.
A reminder that our true destination lies beyond this life
Yes. This world is for sowing; the next for reaping.
questions.rationale: “This general discontentedness is a reminder to everyone that their destination lies somewhere else… that their desired world is not the world before death.”

questions.article: As You Sow, So Shall You Reap
questions.q: What does the article say about those who live with severe and lasting suffering?
options: Their patient endurance will be accepted by God and is enough to win them Paradise
Right. They also serve as reminders to others of this world’s passing nature.
They can expect nothing in either world
Not quite. The article says: Their patient endurance will be accepted by God and is enough to win them Paradise.
They are excused from every duty
Not quite. The article says: Their patient endurance will be accepted by God and is enough to win them Paradise.
Their suffering shows God’s displeasure
Not quite. The article says: Their patient endurance will be accepted by God and is enough to win them Paradise.
questions.rationale: “They may not have been able to perform great deeds, but their patient and silent suffering will be accepted by God… will alone suffice to gain entry into Paradise.”

questions.q: “A politician who complains about the media is like a ship’s captain complaining about the sea.” How does the article apply this to everyone?
options: The media should be ignored
Not quite. The article says: Difficulties are part of life, like waves; the sensible course is to learn to ride over them.
Complaints should be made in private
Not quite. The article says: Difficulties are part of life, like waves; the sensible course is to learn to ride over them.
Difficulties are part of life, like waves; the sensible course is to learn to ride over them
Yes. They train and strengthen us.
People should avoid the sea
Not quite. The article says: Difficulties are part of life, like waves; the sensible course is to learn to ride over them.
questions.rationale: “Instead of complaining about the waves that come our way, we should learn the art of successfully riding over or bypassing them.”

questions.q: The article sorts problems into three kinds by time. What does it advise for each?
options: Present: wait; past: study it; future: fear it
Not quite. The article says: Present: solve by planning and action; past: forget it; future: it does not yet exist.
Present: solve by planning and action; past: forget it; future: it does not yet exist
Correct. Anxiety is a way of thinking, not a physical fact.
All three: ask others for help
Not quite. The article says: Present: solve by planning and action; past: forget it; future: it does not yet exist.
Present: forget it; past: solve it; future: plan it
Not quite. The article says: Present: solve by planning and action; past: forget it; future: it does not yet exist.
questions.rationale: “If it is related to the present, you can solve it through wise planning… If it is related to the past… forget it… If the problem concerns the future, then it is not a problem at all, just a baseless fear.”

questions.q: Ali ibn Abi Talib said, “I realized God by having failed in my planning.” What does the article call this kind of experience, and what does it set beside it?
options: A rare event – beside the rarer miracles
Not quite. The article says: A negative reminder of a power above us – beside the far more numerous positive reminders such as sunrise and rain.
A negative reminder of a power above us – beside the far more numerous positive reminders such as sunrise and rain
Well read. Realisation grows like a tree.
A punishment – beside the rewards of success
Not quite. The article says: A negative reminder of a power above us – beside the far more numerous positive reminders such as sunrise and rain.
A mistake – beside the lessons of books
Not quite. The article says: A negative reminder of a power above us – beside the far more numerous positive reminders such as sunrise and rain.
questions.rationale: “This may be called a negative reminder. There are also positive reminders of the greatness of God and the number of positive reminders is far greater.”

questions.q: Which examples from the Prophet’s years in Madinah does the article offer as a model for relations between Muslims and Jews?
options: A ban on trade between them
Not quite. The article says: Dialogue among the faiths, visits to Jewish leaders and scholars, and standing in respect at a Jewish funeral.
Avoiding all discussion of religion
Not quite. The article says: Dialogue among the faiths, visits to Jewish leaders and scholars, and standing in respect at a Jewish funeral.
Separate quarters for each community
Not quite. The article says: Dialogue among the faiths, visits to Jewish leaders and scholars, and standing in respect at a Jewish funeral.
Dialogue among the faiths, visits to Jewish leaders and scholars, and standing in respect at a Jewish funeral
Yes. “Was he not a human being?”
questions.rationale: “These traditions about the Prophet of Islam give us a model for Muslim-Jewish relations.” The article adds the Quran’s guidance that “reconciliation is the best.”

questions.article: Turn Your Weakness into Your Strength
questions.q: “Man has been created weak,” says the Quran. How does the article see this weakness turning into strength?
options: It disappears with age
Not quite. The article says: It teaches modesty and reliance on others, checks pride, and pushes the mind to develop.
It wins the pity of the strong
Not quite. The article says: It teaches modesty and reliance on others, checks pride, and pushes the mind to develop.
It teaches modesty and reliance on others, checks pride, and pushes the mind to develop
Right. It acts like a “speed-breaker.”
It excuses a person from effort
Not quite. The article says: It teaches modesty and reliance on others, checks pride, and pushes the mind to develop.
questions.rationale: “Weakness makes one realize: ‘I cannot do anything alone’… In this way, weakness, in terms of its results, becomes one’s strength.”

questions.q: A man wanted a house where his costly car need not stand beside a cheap one. What way of thinking does the article recommend instead?
options: To buy a still more costly car
Not quite. The article says: To see a car as a gift from God and from the labour of countless people, beside which one’s own payment is small.
To hide one’s wealth from neighbours
Not quite. The article says: To see a car as a gift from God and from the labour of countless people, beside which one’s own payment is small.
To see a car as a gift from God and from the labour of countless people, beside which one’s own payment is small
Yes. This breeds modesty in place of pride.
To give up owning a car
Not quite. The article says: To see a car as a gift from God and from the labour of countless people, beside which one’s own payment is small.
questions.rationale: “He who considers the thing he has purchased from the market as a divine gift as well as a gift from humanity, and that his own contribution to it is nothing, will certainly develop modesty.”

questions.q: What does the Quran (49:6) ask believers to do on hearing a report about someone?
options: Confront the person at once
Not quite. The article says: Ascertain the facts fully before forming an opinion.
Ascertain the facts fully before forming an opinion
Exactly. Most complaints grow from hearsay and misunderstanding.
Pass it on with a warning
Not quite. The article says: Ascertain the facts fully before forming an opinion.
Believe it if many repeat it
Not quite. The article says: Ascertain the facts fully before forming an opinion.
questions.rationale: “Ascertain the correctness of the report fully, lest you unwittingly harm others, and then regret what you have done.”

questions.q: According to the commentary, when is it shown whether a person is truly a believer?
options: When others are watching
Not quite. The article says: In extraordinary circumstances, when faith calls for sacrifice.
In ordinary daily routine
Not quite. The article says: In extraordinary circumstances, when faith calls for sacrifice.
In old age
Not quite. The article says: In extraordinary circumstances, when faith calls for sacrifice.
In extraordinary circumstances, when faith calls for sacrifice
Well read. There the inner person is revealed.
questions.rationale: “The question of whether a man is a true believer is decided on the basis of how he conducts himself under extraordinary rather than ordinary circumstances.”
